title: Always on: What it’s like being a twenty-something founder in the age of AI
summary: First Round Review explores what it is like being a young founder in the AI era
detailed: “My worst fear is looking back at this time with regret for not taking advantage of the opportunity in front of us,” says Max Brodeur-Urbas.

Brodeur-Urbas shares a similar sentiment with two other twenty-something founders I spoke with who are building in the era of AI: there’s a massive window of opportunity and they’ve got to move fast before it closes.

I spoke with all three to understand what it’s like to be a founder at this age, in this age: where being young gives them an advantage, where experience still matters, and how they decide how much of themselves to give to an opportunity they’re afraid to waste.

sentences: “My worst fear is looking back at this time with regret for not taking advantage of the opportunity in front of us,” says Max Brodeur-Urbas.
He was 24 when he started agent builder Gumloop and has raised $70M since founding three years ago.
“I’m always wondering, ‘What is stopping us from getting this done today?’ I try to shorten timelines as much as I can,” he told me.

Brodeur-Urbas shares a similar sentiment with two other twenty-something founders I spoke with who are building in the era of AI: there’s a massive window of opportunity and they’ve got to move fast before it closes.
Technology keeps expanding what they can build and how quickly they can build it — both for them, and their competition.

“I’m just monomaniacally focused on making sure we’re moving the puck forward,” says Yash Patil, the 23-year-old co-founder of training and inference company Applied Compute, which just agreed to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks in a $4.5 billion all-stock deal.
He spent two years at OpenAI before starting the company at 22 and raising $510M in a little over a year.
And at 24, Adit Abraham left Google to start Reducto, an AI document-parsing startup that raised $108 million within a year and a half.
None of these founders see their age as a disadvantage.
On sales calls, they feel the desire of enterprise executives who want to work with them because of their AI fluency.

With relatively few obligations outside of work, they can dedicate an insane amount of time to their companies — even if their own relationships must take shape around their obligations to their businesses and time away can physically feel uncomfortable.

But they’re still learning how to lead experienced employees, negotiate important contracts and manage their emotions through the ups and downs of running a company where they can see the window closing by the centimeter.
Their employees have bet their careers on the founders’ ability to figure it out.

I spoke with all three to understand what it’s like to be a founder at this age, in this age: where being young gives them an advantage, where experience still matters, and how they decide how much of themselves to give to an opportunity they’re afraid to waste.
“There’s a problem that exists right now that won’t exist in the future — automating the work everyone hates and helping people be more efficient.
We can be a huge player if we do our jobs right.
Or we could just be a blip that tried something and failed,” says Brodeur-Urbas.
The best founders have always been obsessed with their companies.

But the circumstances of the current moment — when anyone can build anything extremely fast, unbound opportunity breeds intense competition — make everything feel so pressing that obsession is almost requisite.
Each of these founders feels like the opportunity to succeed is within their grasp.
But they also feel like there are more hands reaching for it than ever before, with more (and maybe even younger and more AI-pilled) startups spawning every day.
Maintaining perspective is difficult when the ups and downs are felt so viscerally.
“The share of the opportunity is so much larger than any one given company but on a day-to-day basis, it’s so easy to get wrapped up.
Like if you see a competitor in a given deal, it feels like you’re fighting for the same little nugget.
I think as a young founder, it’s harder to zoom out of that perspective,” Abraham says.
Brodeur-Urbas tries not to focus on competitors, but it’s hard when everything about your company feels so personal.
“Any user churning, every win, it feels like it’s tied to who you are,” he says.

“I won’t name them because I don’t talk about our competitors — but when a competing company comes out with something that is very clearly inspired by what we’re doing, chasing the same slice of the pie.

That always feels like shit.”
Even among peers, it can sometimes feel like a real-world X feed.
Brodeur-Urbas is in a group chat of founders but believes that focusing too much on people who are similar causes an echo chamber.

Abraham even finds himself being guarded around other founders, worrying that what he says might make its way through what he calls the VC grapevine: “The number of founder relationships where you can truly be unguarded and talk about your problems earnestly is reasonably limited, which sucks,” he says.

Patil brings a slightly different perspective, describing it more as a “frenemy” dynamic that both fuels pressure but also creates more opportunities than before because there’s so much more surface area.
“The mandates of any one company have expanded.
You’re doing X, and AI lets you do X a lot better and faster.

So now you can do Y too, and you’re going to have more overlap.”
But with ever-expanding competition comes ever-expanding possibility, which Patil was fortunate enough to experience at the frontier.
AI has given Patil opportunities unexpectedly early in life — including the opportunity to work at OpenAI at just 20 years old.
When he was considering leaving Stanford his sophomore year to do so, Sam Altman offered to call Patil’s worried parents to ease their concerns.
He grew up hacking around in Austin, Texas, encouraged by his chip engineer father to build his own coding projects and inspired by his older brother starting his own career in tech.
When he got to Stanford, he spent his first year “funmaxxing” by building lightsabers out of aluminum tubes and a dining hall voting app.

Summer after freshman year, Patil and his friend, eager to tackle a real-world problem instead of tarpit startup ideas centered around college student grievances, turned down internship offers with startups to build something that might land some real paying customers.
They knew their way around the venture capital ecosystem that hovers around Stanford computer science majors, and got several offers for small checks.
But Patil felt iffy about taking “free money,” thinking there would be strings attached if it didn’t work out.
So he sent an email to Sam Altman asking for advice (he’d recently been invited to a dinner for Stanford builders hosted at Altman’s home).
Altman wrote back saying, “I’ll never encourage anyone not to go and build stuff.

If you’re worried about taking someone else’s money, I can fund you for the summer, you can always return the capital if you decide to shut it down.”
Patil and his friend took Altman’s stipend to build an app to help e-commerce companies purge their link rot.
It didn’t work very well, and neither of them ultimately found e-commerce very interesting.
Patil describes it as a “whiteboard company,” a startup idea somewhat arbitrarily plucked off of a brainstorm list.
They wound it down and returned to campus for the fall of 2022.
Then ChatGPT came out, and Patil was mesmerized.
He emailed Altman again, this time inquiring about a job at OpenAI.
Altman encouraged him to apply to their six-month research residency program — which would require him to drop out of school.
Altman’s offer to call was enough to soothe Patil’s parents’ nerves.
“I told my parents that Sam offered to talk to them, and they were like, ‘Oh wow, no, we don't need to take his time.
Just the fact that he wanted to call us is fine,’” he says.
His older brother, on the other hand, told him to go for it.
Patil spent more time at OpenAI than he did at Stanford.

When his colleague Ian Osband found out he wasn’t 21 yet, he planned him a 21st birthday party, featuring a branded party bus, a fat suit for Patil to wear and drinks at the Mission craft cocktail bar Trick Dog, down the street from the OpenAI office.

His experience at OpenAI taught him a lot of things he’s grateful to have learned before he could legally buy a drink: How to work with other people, exposure to real-world problems, what great leadership looks like.
“I got an amazing shot on goal at such a young age, which I was probably undeserving of given my background,” says Patil.
“I didn't even graduate, I didn't even have any AI experience.
